title: Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
The bfi data contain 25 personality items from 2,800 people, five items per Big Five trait. Each item is answered on a 6-point scale from Very inaccurate to Very accurate.
The chosen trait is Neuroticism. The ordered outcome is one Neuroticism item, N4, “Often feel blue” The predictor is a person’s Extraversion subscale score, the mean of E1 to E5 with E1 and E2 reverse-keyed.
I predict that as people are more extraverted, they will give lower responses to “Often feel blue”. Extraversion reflects sociability, high energy, and a predisposition toward positive emotionality, which generally act as a buffer against low mood and negative affect. Therefore, more extraverted individuals should be less likely to report frequently feeling blue than more introverted individuals.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
Data preparation


Code
#Labels for the six response options, from lowest to highest

n_levels <- c("Very inaccurate", "Moderately inaccurate", "Slightly inaccurate", "Slightly accurate", "Moderately accurate", "Very accurate")

#Scoring keys with reverse-keyed items

keys <- list(
  Agreeableness     = c("-A1", "A2", "A3", "A4", "A5"),
  Conscientiousness = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "-C4", "-C5"),
  Extraversion      = c("-E1", "-E2", "E3", "E4", "E5"),
  Neuroticism       = c("N1", "N2", "N3", "N4", "N5"),
  Openness          = c("O1", "-O2", "O3", "O4", "-O5")
)

scores<-scoreItems(keys, data, totals = F, min = 1, max = 6)
scores_df<- scores$scores

data <- data |>
  select(N4) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(scores_df)) |>
  mutate(
    N4 = factor(N4, levels = 1:6, labels = n_levels, ordered = TRUE),
    highest = factor(names(keys)[max.col(scores_df, ties.method = "first")]),
    extra = Extraversion
  ) |>
  drop_na(N4, extra, highest) |>
  mutate(extra_c = extra - mean(extra))
n_analysed <- nrow(data)
extra_sd <- sd(data$extra)
extra_bar <- mean(data$extra)


All 25 personality items were verified and stored as integers before scoring. Each Big Five subscale was scored using psych::scoreItems() as the mean of its five items on the 1–6 scale after reverse-scoring negatively keyed items (with missing item responses within subscales imputed at the item median by default). After removing participants with missing values on the analysis variables, the final analytic sample was N = 2,764. Before centring, the mean Extraversion score was 4.14 (SD = 1.06).

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
section: How the predictor relates to the responses
text:
How the predictor relates to the responses


Code
plot_jitter<-ggplot(data, aes(extra, as.numeric(N4), colour = N4)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6, labels = n_levels) +
  labs(title = "Higher Extraversion, less likely to endorse 'Often feel blue', with overlap",
       x = "Extraversion (subscale mean, 1-6)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
plot_jitter









The jittered dot plot reveals a clear downward pattern accompanied by substantial individual overlap. Respondents with lower Extraversion scores are concentrated more heavily in the “accurate” categories (Slightly accurate through Very accurate), whereas respondents with higher Extraversion scores cluster more densely in Very inaccurate and Moderately inaccurate. Because the outcome consists of six discrete, ordered labels rather than an interval-scaled measurement, the psychological spacing between adjacent options is not equal. Fitting an ordinary linear regression could produce a single point prediction such as “3.4” or values outside 1 to 6, so an appropriate model should instead estimate a valid probability for each of the six categories that sums to 1.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
text:
An unordered outcome
Each person’s dominant trait (their highest of the five subscale scores) is a set of categories with no built-in order. Being highest on Openness is not “more” than being highest on Agreeableness. An outcome like this requires a baseline-category (multinomial) model, such as nnet::multinom(), rather than clm().


Code
ordered_dat <- data |>
  count(highest) |>
  mutate(highest = fct_reorder(highest, n))

unordered_plot <- ggplot(ordered_dat, aes(highest, n)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "maroon") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Dominant trait: five categories with no order", 
       x = NULL, y = "People") +
  theme_minimal()
unordered_plot

For a person of average Extraversion, the most likely single response is Moderately inaccurate (P = 0.246, or 24.57%). Their probability of endorsing the item, that is, responding “Slightly accurate” or higher, is 1 - P(Y <= “Slightly inaccurate”) = 1 - 0.557 = 0.443 (44.33%).

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
section: 4b. Comparing and interpreting the chosen model
text:
4b. Comparing and interpreting the chosen model
The slope, beta = -0.644, is on the latent logit scale. A one-point increase in Extraversion moves a person’s latent tendency to feel blue as reflected by N4 down by 0.644. The middle categories are each about 0.87 units wide on that scale, so one point of Extraversion shifts someone by roughly 73.67% of a middle category.

title: Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
Ordinal Logistic Regression Assignment
section: 7b. Coefficient plot of cumulative odds ratios
text:
7b. Coefficient plot of cumulative odds ratios
The plot shows the shared proportional-odds OR alongside the threshold-specific ORs from Section 5, so it also works as a visual check of proportional odds.


Code
bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Threshold = "Shared (proportional odds)", OR = or_tab$estimate,
         low = or_tab$conf.low, high = or_tab$conf.high, type = "Shared"),
  threshold_or |> transmute(Threshold, OR, low, high, type = "Threshold-specific")
) |>
  mutate(
    Threshold = fct_rev(fct_inorder(Threshold))) |>
  ggplot(aes(OR, Threshold, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + 
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative odds ratios per point of Extraversion",
       x = "Odds ratio (responding above the threshold)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Every interval sits well below 1 (the dashed line). The threshold-specific estimates also cluster around the shared estimate, which is what proportional odds implies.
